profile.summary: This is the evaluation in the FramePool paper, not a released suite. Two massively parallel reporter assay test sets of 5' UTR sequences with measured mean ribosome load are used to compare frame pooling against the published Optimus 5-Prime models: one of 20,000 random sequences all 50 nucleotides long, and one of 7,600 random sequences of 25 to 100 nucleotides. The same two length settings are also reported on truncated human 5' UTRs measured in the same experiment. Scores are Pearson correlations between predicted and observed mean ribosome load, and the point of the comparison is how well a model generalises to sequences longer than those it was trained on.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Evaluating frame pooling on MPRA data; Methods, Model testing

summary_quotes.text: Two MPRA test sets were used to evaluate model performance. One consists of 20,000 MPRA sequences that are 50 nt long. The other consists of 7,600 MPRA sequences, which vary in length from 25 to 100 nt, with 100 sequences for each length.

These are the same test sets which were used in Sample et al. [<xref rid="pcbi.1008982.ref025" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>] to evaluate the performance of the Optimus models. Thus, performances on these sets are directly comparable.
A similar pattern can be observed on (truncated) human sequences measured in the MPRA experiments (<xref ref-type="supplementary-material" rid="pcbi.1008982.s001">S1 Fig</xref>).

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How accurately a model predicts mean ribosome load, a proxy for translation rate, from a 5' UTR sequence, and in particular whether it still works on sequences longer than its training data. The question matters because the earlier Optimus models learn position-specific weights relative to the start codon, so longer UTRs must be truncated: by the authors' count of GENCODE v19, only 30% of human 5' UTRs are 100 nucleotides or shorter and the median is about 200, so truncation usually throws away more than half the sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Results, Modelling 5'UTR of any length using frame pooling

quotes.text: a model was trained on a massively parallel reporter assay to predict mean ribosome load (MRL)—a proxy for translation rate—directly from 5’UTR sequence with a high degree of accuracy. However, this model is restricted to sequence lengths investigated in the reporter assay
the Optimus models learn position-specific weights (where the position is defined relative to the canonical start codon)
It was found that only 30% of 5’UTR are 100 nt or shorter.
as the median sequence has about 200 nt, it means that truncation will usually lead to a substantial loss of information

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data come from the Sample et al. reporter assay, not from this study. More than 200,000 entirely random 50-nucleotide 5' UTRs were fused to an enhanced green fluorescent protein coding sequence and their mean ribosome load measured by polysome profiling, with a second library of about 80,000 random UTRs of varying length. The test sets are the held-out sets from that study: 20,000 sequences of 50 nucleotides, and 7,600 sequences of 25 to 100 nucleotides with 100 per length. Of the 260,000 sequences in the fixed-length library, 20,000 were withheld as a validation set used for hyperparameters and early stopping and not for testing. The human comparison uses human 5' UTRs that were measured in the same reporter experiment, truncated to the two length settings.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, Model training and Model testing; Results

Using the polysome profiling technique, the mean ribosome load (MRL), a metric of the average number of ribosomes associated to a given RNA and a proxy for translation efficiency, was measured for each sequence.
This set comprises the sequences of 260,000 random 5’UTR, all 50 nucleotides in length, together with mean ribosome load measurements for each sequence.
Of these 260,000 sequences, 20,000 were withheld for the validation set, which was employed to optimize hyperparameters and for early stopping (but not for testing).
The FramePool100 model was trained on the random variable length MPRA dataset. This set comprises 76,319 random 5’UTR, with lengths varying from 25 to 100 nucleotides

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model predicts mean ribosome load for each test sequence and the score is the Pearson correlation with the measured value; the comparison is made against the Optimus models' published numbers on the same held-out sets. Training uses the Adam optimizer with mean squared error loss and early stopping after three epochs without validation improvement, keeping the model with the lowest validation error, while the variable-length and combined models were trained for six epochs straight with no early stopping. Alongside the two main models the authors train frame-unaware controls (global pooling and two dilated convolution variants on the same training set) and k-mer random forests, including one given frame-separated k-mer counts, to separate the benefit of frame information from the benefit of deep learning.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Evaluating frame pooling on MPRA data; Methods, Model training, Frame unaware deep learning models and Random forest models

quotes.text: the predictions of the frame pooling model (FramePool50) show a Pearson correlation of 0.964 with the observed MRL values, whereas Optimus50 had a correlation of 0.966 (<xref ref-type="fig" rid="pcbi.1008982.g002">Fig 2</xref>)

Training was done using the Adam optimizer with default parameters and a standard mean-squared-error loss function. Training was stopped early if no improvement was made on the validation set for 3 consecutive epochs.
No new validation set was constructed for this data and training was done for six epochs straight, without early stopping or other optimizations.
we trained three models, which we call global_pool_conv, dilated_conv and more_dilated_conv, respectively
This random forest takes as input the k-mer-counts for each frame (giving a vector of length 3*(4^k)).

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the 50-nucleotide random test set the two models are level: FramePool50 at 0.964 against Optimus50 at 0.966. On the 25 to 100 nucleotide random test set Optimus50 falls to 0.743 while FramePool50 holds 0.901, close to Optimus100's 0.915, which was trained on variable-length data. The human sequences follow the same pattern: 0.882 for FramePool50 against 0.889 for Optimus50 at 50 nucleotides, and 0.871 against 0.7 at 25 to 100 nucleotides. The authors read this as frame pooling giving up almost nothing in the fixed-length setting while generalising to longer sequences.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Evaluating frame pooling on MPRA data; Fig 2 caption

quotes.text: On these 20,000 sequences, the predictions of the frame pooling model (FramePool50) show a Pearson correlation of 0.964 with the observed MRL values, whereas Optimus50 had a correlation of 0.966 (<xref ref-type="fig" rid="pcbi.1008982.g002">Fig 2</xref>).

As a result, it generalizes poorly to this variable-length test set, and the correlation drops to 0.743. FramePool50, despite being trained on the same data, does not face this restriction and generalizes much better, with a correlation of 0.901 (<xref ref-type="fig" rid="pcbi.1008982.g002">Fig 2</xref>).

Note that this result compares well even with Optimus100, which was trained on the variable-length MPRA data, and has a correlation of 0.915 with the observed values of this test set (<xref ref-type="supplementary-material" rid="pcbi.1008982.s020">S1 Table</xref>).

Optimus50 and FramePool50 perform very similarly on human 5’UTR truncated to 50 nt (Pearson correlation: 0.889 vs 0.882), but frame pooling again generalizes better: for 25–100 nt sequences the correlation for Optimus50 drops to 0.7, whereas FramePool50 remains at 0.871.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository, download the Zenodo deposit, put its data dictionary in the Data directory and run the training notebook; to reproduce the paper's plots without rerunning predictions, unpack the prediction archive into Data/Predictions and run the validation notebook. For predicting on new sequences the model is published through the Kipoi model zoo, with a dataloader that takes a BED file of 5' UTR exon regions, a VCF of variants and a reference FASTA, injects each variant and reports the log2 fold change in predicted mean ribosome load, plus the same figure for a simulated frameshift.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md. Paper: Methods, Kipoi integration; Data Availability. Zenodo record: file list

quotes.text: To replicate the main results, clone the repository. Next download the data from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3584237. Place the data_dict.pkl in the Data directory. Then you can run the Model_Training.ipynb notebook to train a Framepool model.
If you would like to generate the paper plots, without running predictions, place the contents of the Predictions.tar.gz file in Data/Predictions and then run the Validations.ipynb notebook.
The dataloader takes as input a bed file specifying 5’UTR exon regions of interest, a vcf file specifying the variants of interest, and a fasta file with a human reference genome.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Optimus50 and Optimus100 from Sample et al. are the published comparators. The authors add their own controls: three frame-unaware convolutional models (global_pool_conv with conventional global max and average pooling, plus dilated_conv and more_dilated_conv), and k-mer random forests (3-mer and 4-mer, a framed forest using per-frame k-mer counts, a hyperparameter-optimised framed forest and a 5-mer version), all trained on the same training set as FramePool50.

quotes.text: The first, global_pool_conv used the same hyperparameters as FramePool50, but the frame pooling layer was replaced with conventional global max and average pooling.
We trained two such random forest models: 3mer_random_forest and 4mer_random_forest, which use 3-mer and 4-mer counts as input features, respectively.
All these models were trained on the same training set as FramePool50.
S4 Table</label><caption><title>Performance on MPRA datasets of different random forest models.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Test sequences are held out and are reused unchanged from the earlier study, and the validation set is kept separate from the test set. The sequences in the two main sets are entirely random, so there is no homology between train and test to control for. No further control is described: in particular nothing is said about overlap between the human sequences used here and anything in training, and the paper does not say how the 7,600 variable-length test sequences relate to the 76,319 sequences the variable-length model was trained on.

facts.value: A massively parallel reporter assay read out by polysome profiling: each 5' UTR is fused to an eGFP coding sequence and the mean ribosome load, the average number of ribosomes on a transcript, is measured. facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The 5' UTR sequence alone, one-hot encoded. Optimus models additionally require the sequence to be at or below their training length, which is the restriction under test; the frame pooling model takes any length. For variant work through Kipoi the inputs are a reference and a variant sequence built from a genome FASTA, a BED of UTR exons and a VCF.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised training from scratch on the assay data. FramePool50 was trained on the fixed-length library with manual hyperparameter tuning and early stopping, FramePool100 on the variable-length library for six epochs, and a combined model on both with a library indicator to account for scaling differences. Nothing is scored zero-shot.

quotes.text: The FramePool50 model was trained on the egfp1 MPRA dataset from Sample et al. [<xref rid="pcbi.1008982.ref025" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>].
The FramePoolCombined model was trained on both training sets for six epochs straight, with an additional library indicator to account for differences in scaling.

run_guide.summary: Clone the repository, download the Zenodo deposit, and run the published notebooks to train a frame pooling model or to regenerate the paper's plots from saved predictions.
prerequisites: The repository's notebooks, which need a Jupyter environment; the sources read do not list package versions for the modelling code.
The Zenodo deposit at 10.5281/zenodo.3584237, which holds data_dict.pkl, the trained Framepool_combined_residual.h5 model and Predictions.tar.gz, under CC BY 4.0.
For the Kipoi route, a human reference genome FASTA, a BED file of 5' UTR exon regions and a VCF of variants; the dataloader is written for Python 3.6 with numpy, pandas and pybedtools.

Points for a human. First, the two human entries carry no size: the article text gives their correlations but their counts appear only in S1 Fig, which was not fetched. Second, the two random sizes are the test-set sizes as the Methods print them (20,000 and 7,600), not the library sizes (260,000 and 76,319), which are quoted separately. Third, the Zenodo DOI in the paper (10.5281/zenodo.3584237) is the concept DOI; the API response returned record 3584925 of 19 December 2019, which is the version read here, and the released date comes from that record, not from the article. Fourth, the record's existing sources include Supplementary Tables S1 and S4 as XLSX files; those were not fetched because an XLSX cannot be quoted as text, so the full model tables are not covered. Fifth, the paper's wider analyses (endogenous genes, variant effects, uTIS motifs) are not part of the four protocols stored against this record.
